bug_description.normalized: The exact staged 643-byte `poc` is a raw NCP-UART witness that, on the reproduced vulnerable run, drives OpenThread far enough to deliver a CoAP Server Data request into `Leader::HandleServerData()`. That handler extracts the current request's `ThreadNetworkDataTlv` into stack `networkData` and forwards `networkData.GetTlvs()` / `networkData.GetLength()` plus a sender-derived RLOC16 into `RegisterNetworkData()`. `RegisterNetworkData()` first validates the current TLVs for that RLOC with `RlocLookup(aRloc16, rlocIn, rlocStable, aTlvs, aTlvsLength, kMatchModeRloc16, false)`, then calls `RlocLookup(aRloc16, rlocIn, unused, mTlvs, mLength, kMatchModeRloc16)` on existing leader state without clearing the reused `rlocIn` flag. The subsequent `if (rlocIn)` therefore proves only that `rlocIn` was true after one or both lookups; the staged artifacts do not show whether that truth came from the current TLVs, from `mTlvs`, or from both. The saved ASan report identifies `networkData` in `HandleServerData()` as the over-read stack object, which, together with the `||` short-circuit at line 760, proves the crash occurred in the second comparison `IsStableUpdated(mTlvs, mLength, aTlvs, aTlvsLength)`: the first arm returned false, and the second arm uses the current stack TLVs as `aTlvsBase`. Inside that second call, iteration over `mTlvs` reaches a stored stable Prefix TLV with a stable `borderRouter`; `FindPrefix(...)` locates the matching current prefix in `networkData`, and `FindBorderRouter(*prefixBase, true)` returns the current stable `borderRouterBase` inside that same stack object. The vulnerable condition then calls `memcmp(borderRouter, borderRouterBase, borderRouter->GetLength())` without first requiring equal TLV lengths. For this witness the stored Border Router TLV is longer than the current one, so the stored `borderRouter->GetLength()` makes `memcmp` read past `borderRouterBase` and into the redzone after stack `networkData`, matching the saved AddressSanitizer stack-buffer-overflow READ of size 8 at `src/core/thread/network_data_leader_ftd.cpp:638`. The fixing diff adds the missing same-length guard before both Border Router and Has Route `memcmp` calls, so the reproduced Border Router path would return `rval = true` instead of over-reading the current stack buffer. The staged artifacts do not identify which earlier UART frame or prior leader state created the longer stored TLV.

tainted_value_origin.description: The current stack-resident Thread Network Data byte span and length later become `aTlvsBase` / `aTlvsBaseLength` and the shorter `borderRouterBase` operand in the crashing second `IsStableUpdated(...)` call.

sink.description: AddressSanitizer sink. The comparison uses the stored Border Router TLV's length while `borderRouterBase` points into the shorter current `networkData` stack buffer.
sink.note: Stage 01 reproduces `AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow READ of size 8` here and reports that the over-read object is stack `networkData` in `HandleServerData()` at line 154.

root_cause.description: The Border Router comparison only checks whether `borderRouterBase` is null before calling `memcmp`; it never requires the two TLVs to have equal `GetLength()` values first.
root_cause.note: The fixing diff adds the missing guard `(borderRouter->GetLength() != borderRouterBase->GetLength())` ahead of `memcmp` on this path. With that extra check, the witness would return `rval = true` without reading past the current stack `networkData` buffer.

parser_admitted.description: The current request has already passed Thread TLV lookup and the vacuous `networkData.IsValid()` check, so leader-side registration now begins on the attacker-controlled Network Data bytes.

existing_rloc_state.description: The crashing second `IsStableUpdated(...)` call is only reachable if `if (rlocIn)` evaluates true at line 758. Because `rlocIn` is reused across the two `RlocLookup` calls and is not cleared before the second one, the staged artifacts prove only that `rlocIn` remained true after those lookups, not whether that truth came from the current `aTlvs`, from `mTlvs`, or from both.

fine_trace.note: Source. `ThreadTlv::GetTlv` copies the current request's attacker-controlled Thread Network Data TLV into stack `networkData`, making its nested network-data bytes and outer length field available to the leader-side parser.

The handler derives `aRloc16` from the sender address's low 16 bits and forwards the current stack buffer into `RegisterNetworkData()`. In the crashing second comparison this same buffer becomes `aTlvsBase` / `borderRouterBase`.

fine_trace.code: SuccessOrExit(error = RlocLookup(aRloc16, rlocIn, rlocStable, aTlvs, aTlvsLength, kMatchModeRloc16, /* aAllowOtherEntries */ false));
fine_trace.note: Registration parses the current TLVs and only continues if their Border Router / Has Route entries are compatible with the same sender-derived `aRloc16`; otherwise the function exits before any stability comparison occurs.

fine_trace.code: RlocLookup(aRloc16, rlocIn, unused, mTlvs, mLength, kMatchModeRloc16);
fine_trace.note: The second lookup scans existing leader state using the same `rlocIn` out-parameter from step 3. `RlocLookup` only assigns `aIn = true` on matches and does not clear it, so after this call `rlocIn` means only that it is true after one or both lookups, not specifically that this second lookup found a same-RLOC entry in `mTlvs`.

depends_on.via: RlocLookup(aRloc16, rlocIn, rlocStable, aTlvs, aTlvsLength, kMatchModeRloc16, false)

fine_trace.note: The update path is entered because `rlocIn` is true at this branch. From the staged artifacts and exact source, that truth could come from the current `aTlvs` lookup, the `mTlvs` lookup, or both.

fine_trace.var: IsStableUpdated(aTlvs, aTlvsLength, mTlvs, mLength), IsStableUpdated(mTlvs, mLength, aTlvs, aTlvsLength)
fine_trace.code: if (IsStableUpdated(aTlvs, aTlvsLength, mTlvs, mLength) || IsStableUpdated(mTlvs, mLength, aTlvs, aTlvsLength))
fine_trace.note: Inside the update path, the code checks stable-data differences in both directions. The saved ASan report names current stack `networkData` as the over-read object, so the crashing call must be the second arm `IsStableUpdated(mTlvs, mLength, aTlvs, aTlvsLength)`: the first arm returned false, otherwise `||` would short-circuit before the second arm ran.

In the second call, `aTlvs` is stored leader state `mTlvs`. When iteration reaches the relevant stored Prefix TLV, `FindBorderRouter(*prefix, true)` returns the stored stable Border Router sub-TLV whose `GetLength()` is later reused as the `memcmp` byte count.
The vulnerable comparison block is only entered for a stable Prefix TLV and either no Context TLV or a present stable Border Router TLV. The witness takes this block for the stored prefix.

The stored prefix bytes are searched in `aTlvsBase`, which in the crashing second arm is the current stack `networkData` buffer. A matching Prefix TLV must be found there; otherwise execution takes `ExitNow(rval = true)` and skips `memcmp`.

Inside the current matching prefix, the code finds the stable Border Router sub-TLV in the current request. This pointer aliases bytes inside stack `ThreadNetworkDataTlv networkData`, the exact stack object ASan later reports as over-read.

Root cause. The Border Router comparison only checks `borderRouterBase` for null before comparing raw TLV bytes; it does not require `borderRouter->GetLength() == borderRouterBase->GetLength()`. The fix adds exactly that missing equality test before `memcmp`.

Sink. `memcmp` uses the stored Border Router TLV's longer `GetLength()` while `borderRouterBase` points into the shorter current `networkData` stack buffer. That size mismatch makes the compare read past the end of `networkData`, matching ASan's `stack-buffer-overflow READ of size 8` on the `networkData` stack object in `HandleServerData()`.

cross_validation.trace_consistent_with_stack: The saved ASan stack directly covers fine-trace steps 6-12 (`RegisterNetworkData -> IsStableUpdated -> memcmp`). Earlier extraction/admission steps 1-5 are reconstructed from the sole `HandleServerData` call site that forwards `networkData` into `RegisterNetworkData()`, the paired `RlocLookup` calls, and the `if (rlocIn)` gate that must be true before either `IsStableUpdated(...)` arm can run.
cross_validation.patch_resolves_note: The fixing diff inserts `(borderRouter->GetLength() != borderRouterBase->GetLength())` and the analogous Has Route guard before the two `memcmp` calls. On this witness's Border Router path, that added length check would stop at line 638 with `rval = true` instead of reading past current stack `networkData`.

format.name: raw NCP-UART byte stream
format.contract: The trigger contract is the exact staged 643-byte raw NCP-UART stream saved as `poc` (SHA256 `0e2bf6541100da91751e592b69411ab2d5e1cdb1152866f75f39d9952671ca9a`). On the witnessed path it reaches a leader-side Server Data request whose current Thread Network Data TLV becomes stack `networkData` / `aTlvsBase`, while `mTlvs` contains a stable Prefix/BorderRouter pair with the same prefix and a longer stable Border Router TLV. The second `IsStableUpdated(mTlvs, mLength, aTlvs, aTlvsLength)` call then finds the current matching prefix and its shorter stable Border Router TLV inside `networkData` and evaluates `memcmp(borderRouter, borderRouterBase, borderRouter->GetLength())`, producing the reproduced over-read. The staged artifacts do not establish which earlier frame or preexisting state created the stored longer TLV, so this contract stays at the exact witnessed semantics and does not generalize to arbitrary NCP-UART traffic.
